chunks: Al-Hussein ibn Ahmad ibn Idris - may God be pleased with him - narrated that his father quoted Muhammad ibn Ahmad, on the authority of Musa ibn Ja’far ibn Wahab al-Baghdady, on the authority of Ubaydullah al-Dihqan, on the authority of Ahmad ibn Umar al-Halabi, on the authority of Zayd al-Qatat, on the authority of Aban ibn Taqlib that he had heard Aba Abdullah (peace be upon him) say:
Maintaining health is the result of careful examinations, feeling sorry is the result of rushing, and not getting things done on time is the result of not starting on time.

key_terms.التَّثَبُّت: Deliberation, carefulness, or taking one's time

ai.seo_question: What is the relationship between haste, deliberation, and the timing of actions in Shia ethics?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Khisal*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes a causal link between deliberation (*tathabbut*) and safety, contrasting it with the regret born of haste (*'ajala*). This teaching underscores the Shia emphasis on *hikmah* (wisdom) and timing, suggesting that the spiritual and practical efficacy of an action is intrinsically tied to its proper execution in time. The final clause highlights that premature initiation disrupts the natural order of fulfillment, a concept resonating with the divine measure (*mīzān*) in creation.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 3-52 Al-Hussein ibn Ahmad ibn Idris - may God be pleased with him - narrated that his father quoted Muhammad ibn Ahmad, on the authority of Musa ibn Ja’far ibn Wahab al-Baghdady, on the authority of Ubaydullah al-Dihqan, on the authority of Ahmad ibn Umar al-Halabi, on the authority of Zayd al-Qatat, on the authority of Aban ibn Taqlib that he had heard Aba Abdullah as-Sadiq (MGB) say, “
Maintaining health is the result of careful examinations, feeling sorry is the result of rushing, and not getting things done on time is the result of not starting on time.”
